chunks.content: 1. Introduction Mobile phones were first introduced into the market in the 1970s with no pre-market safety testing [ ]. As most users were adult male medical and military personnel, the average call was assumed to last six minutes and was judged safe if it resulted in no increase in temperature from the weak non-ionizing radiation emitted. Today, very young persons or those with much smaller brains and bodies in comparison to the 175 cm tall, 88 kg male phantom against which phones were first tested for their capacity to change temperature, use more than half of the world’s nearly 7 billion phones. Because they are often held directly next to the head and pulsed digital radiation is absorbed about 2 cm into the brain, the effects of mobile phones particularly on the central nervous system may be remarkable. Biological agents can be thought of as having two distinct types of impacts: those that constitute direct physical impacts such as change in structure, cell count, proteomics, etc.; and those that constitute functional or behavioral effects such as change in response time, memory, or other standardized measure of performance that have been well characterized through a battery of tests [ ]. Previous investigations have confirmed a number of important structural impacts of EMF. A decrease in the number of Purkinje cells in the rats exposed to a 900 MHz electromagnetic field (EMF) was previously reported [ ]. Additionally, a significant decrease in the number of granular and pyramidal cells of the hippocampus, which play a key role in memory-related functions, was shown by stereological techniques that allow 3-dimensional imaging of location [ ]. Other destructive effects have also been determined by different methods. Damage to the cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus, and basal ganglia have resulted from neuronal damage induced by exposure to a 900 MHz EMF [ ]. Other studies have demonstrated critical functional changes after EMF exposures. The effect of EMF exposure on increasing permeability of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) has been well documented for more than four decades [ ]. This increased permeability affects homeostasis and may cause leakage of serum albumin into brain tissue. This process also leads to neuronal degeneration in the brain [ ]. Currently, this property of EMF/RF is being used for enhanced uptake of chemotherapy in the treatment of brain cancer, while amplitude modulated current is being employed as part of a treatment involving tumor-treating fields (TTF) that can interfere with post-mitotic spindle formation and increase survival of seriously ill brain and pancreas cancer patients [ ]. Exogenous influences such as extra-low-frequency electromagnetic field (EMF) have been shown to effect pain and inflammation by modulating G-protein receptors, down-regulating cyclooxygenase-2 activity, and affecting the calcium/calmodulin/nitric oxide pathway. Investigators have reported changes in opioid receptors and second messengers, such as cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), in opiate tolerance and dependence by showing how repeated exposure to morphine decreases adenylate cyclase activity causing cAMP to return to control levels in the tolerant state, and increase above control levels during withdrawal [ ]. In addition, other functional impacts of EMF exposure may affect neuronal membranes and organelles, such as lysosomes and mitochondria; consequently, heavy metals and reactive oxygen species (ROS) may reach high levels in intracellular areas [ ]. Thus, electromagnetic radiation-induced tissue damage may be associated with ROS. In this context, one of the several molecular pathways involved in EMF exposure-induced neuronal damage is the caspase3-dependent pathway [ ]. The extracellular signal-regulated protein kinases 1 and 2 (ERK1/2) pathway also plays a crucial role in signal transduction regarding cell growth and differentiation [ ]. Friedman et al. have effectively shown that MAP-kinase are also affected by low levels of EMF/RF and thus electromagnetic radiation emitted from mobile phones may induce the ERK cascade and the other cellular processes [ ]. Neuronal ultrastructural effects of EMF exposure on these pathways have been investigated using proper immunohistochemical and electron microscopic analyses in a study conducted by Tang et al. [ ]. The hippocampus and parietal cortex revealed tight and regular formation of neurons with neuroglia cells in the non-exposed group. Electron microscopic analysis in the group exposed to 900 MHz EMF for 28 days showed many empty and inadequate areas surrounded by vessels and neurons [ ]. Moreover, this is consistent with many studies showing the harmful effects of EMF on the developing nervous system during prenatal and postnatal periods [ ]. In particular, EMF exposure can lead to neuronal death and inhibits transformation of neuronal stem cells into neurons [ ]. After electromagnetic radiation (EMR), the presence of increased free radicals causes the deterioration of membrane integrity by acting on proteins and nucleic acids. This also leads to some gene mutations and antioxidant defenses, which occur to counter these effects [ ]. Measurement of ROS to determine these effects is very difficult due to their high reactivity, short half-life, and high concentrations. The intracellular damage activates superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT) and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) [ ]. The first enzymatic defense against to the ROS is SOD [ ]. CAT produces a peroxidative reaction in the presence of low levels of H 2 O 2 and high concentrations of free electron donors [ ]. Normally, the main enzyme responsible for the detoxification of H 2 O 2 is GSH-Px, and it inhibits lipid peroxidation. GSH-Px produces H 2 O 2 from water by reducing GSH [ ]. By means of this reaction, GSH becomes oxidized glutathione (GSSG) [ ]. Many studies have examined both the neuroprotective effects of some antioxidants as well as the damaging impacts of EMF. In term of this point, the efficiency of melatonin (Mel) and omega-3 (ω3) to induce repair or otherwise interfere with the damaging effects of EMF is noteworthy. Research shows that Mel is an antioxidant agent, as well as ω3 [ ]. As a free radical scavenger, Mel has a high degree of lipophilicity and therefore does not require any binding receptor for its effects [ ]. Additionally, ω3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (ω3 PUFAs) are an essential type of fatty acids and play a crucial role in neurological function because they are integral membrane components and energy substrates [ ]. A few studies have been done using stereological techniques to evaluate the effect of EMF exposure on the CNS. In addition, structural changes after prenatal exposures to a 900 MHz EMF have been investigated by several studies [ ]. However, there are no enough studies regarding evaluation of EMF exposure on the cellular number in the brain and cerebellum of the rats using quantitative techniques. In this context, the present study was designed to investigate the structural and functional impacts of EMF radiation on the brain. In addition, the possible neuroprotective effects of Mel and ω3 have also been searched against EMF exposure. 2. Material and methods The main purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of 900 MHz EMF exposure and the possible neuroprotective effects of the Mel and ω3 on the granular and pyramidal cells in the hippocampus and Purkinje and granular cells in the cerebellum of adult rats. Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) are two important fatty acids that can be found in fish oil [ ], and for this reason fish oil is an important nutritional source. To obtain reliable data for EMF exposure and the neuroprotective ability of these substances, the optical fractionator method – which is a type of unbiased stereological probing technique – paired with cognitive tests and biochemical parameters of oxidative stress. Electrophysiological analysis may inform us about sensitive alterations of interactions in the brain. In this context, electrophysiological assessment was also used in the present study. We employed two overall methods to evaluate both structural and functional impacts on the young animal brain and their subsequent performance [ ]. Prior to sacrifice, animal behaviors were evaluated by the passive avoidance test [ ], where animals were trained to avoid a noxious stimulant such as an electric shock for a food reward. In this behavioral test, three parts were conducted, including an exploration test (1), a learning test (2) and a retention test (3). The exploration test was conducted in three trials. The rats were kept in the center of the light compartment and the door was kept open for 3 min. The total time to enter the dark compartment was noted for each trial. When the rats entered the dark compartment, the door between the compartments was closed and 0.5 mA electric shock was given for 3 s. Then, the ceiling was opened and the rats were returned to the home cage. Each rat received retention tests that were applied after the 24 and 48 h of 0.5 mA electric shock. After perfusion, the routine histological procedures were applied for the brain and cerebellum, which had been removed from the cranium [ ]. Numbers of cells in the stained sections were estimated using the optical fractionator technique, which permits identification of both cell number and membrane integrity. 2.1. Animals and experimental design Experiments in the present study were approved by the Experimental Animal Studies Ethics Committee of Ondokuz Mayis University (2013/20; 05.06.2013). The adult male Wistar albino rats (n = 24), 12 week-old, and 230–280 g, were separately housed in special cages consisting of glass ceilings and plastic floors. During the study, rats were maintained at room temperature (22 ± 2°C), with 40%–50% relative humidity under a 12/12-h light/dark cycle. The rats were fed tap water and standard rat chow. This study had four groups that consist of electromagnetic field (EMF) exposed group (n = 6), electromagnetic field exposed + melatonin treated group (EMF + Mel) (n = 6), electromagnetic field exposed + omega-3 (ω3) (n = 6) treated group (EMF + ω3) and control group (Cont) (n = 6). The Cont group was not exposed to any procedure, the EMF group was exposed to a 900 MHz EMF for 1 h/day, the EMF + Mel group was given 50 mg/kg/day Mel (Sigma-Aldrich Comp., St. Louis, MO, USA) injected intraperitoneally (i.p.) while receiving 900 MHz EMF exposure [ ] and the EMF + ω3 animals were fed with standard feed plus an additional 10% of Ω3 substances (Sigma Chemical Co., St. Louis, MO, USA) while receiving the same EMF exposure. Rats were first exposed at 12 weeks of age and weighed 230–280 g on the first day of exposure ( ). In the laboratory conditions, the technicians were advised to keep their mobile phones turned off during the experimental process. The rats were placed in a Faraday cage, which blocks electric fields and electromagnetic waves. 2.2.1. Exposure system The EMF exposure system included a round plastic cage with 16 separate parts (diameter 5.5 cm, length 12 cm), an EMF meter, and a monopole antenna. The signal generator was operated at 2 W (Electromagnetic Compatibility Laboratory, Süleyman Demirel University, Isparta, Turkey), and the heads of rats were placed in close proximity to the probe. The rats of EMF (n = 6), EMF + Mel (n = 6) and EMF + ω3 (n = 6) groups were passively constrained to keep their heads near the exposure, while 900 MHz of continuously modulated wave electromagnetic energy (peak specific absorption rate [SAR] 2 W/kg, average power density 1 ± 0.4 mW/cm 2 ) was emitted [ ]. The specific absorption rate was obtained from the estimated numerical calculations [ ]. The rats were exposed to 900 MHz of EMF for 60 min/day (4:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m.) for 15 days. 2.3. Cardiac perfusion and tissue preparation Following the exposure period and passive avoidance tests, the rats were anesthetized with ketamine (5 mg/kg i.p.) and Xylazin (2 mg/kg i.p.). Cardiac perfusion was performed with 10% neutral buffered formalin while the heartbeat continued. Following the perfusion, the brain and cerebellum were processed in graded alcohols (70% to 100%) and xylene, and embedded in paraffin for sectioning. Sections of the hippocampus and cerebellum were taken with a rotary microtome (Leica RM 2135; Leica Instruments, Nussloch, Germany). Next, using systematic random sampling, 20 μm thick serial sections were obtained from paraffin-embedded blocks in the sagittal plane. One out of every six sections was selected for analysis, placed on coated slides, and stained with cresyl violet. 2.4. The coefficient of error (CE) for a subject was considered ≤ 0.05 for appropriate sampling. CE and coefficient variation (CV) values are important for the appropriate estimation. The first section in the series was chosen at random from the first six sections, and then every sixth section was collected in a systematic manner. Therefore, the section-sampling fraction was given as 1/6. A total of 16–23 sections were obtained from each brain and cerebellum for adequate estimation with the optical fractionator [ ]. For analyzing the number of granular cells in the dentate gyrus of hippocampus (DG), the counting-frame size was 100 μm 2 and the sampling grid area was 22.500 μm 2 . For analyzing the number of pyramidal cells in the hippocampus, the counting frame was 1600 μm 2 and the sampling grid area was 22.500 μm 2 . For analyzing the number of granular cells in the cerebellum, the counting frame was 625 μm 2 and the sampling grid area was 90.000 μm 2 . Finally, for analyzing the number of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum, the counting frame was 1600 μm 2 and the grid sampling area was 22.500 μm 2 . 2.5. Passive avoidance apparatus and tasks The passive avoidance test apparatus consisted of two compartments − dark and light. A 7 × 7 cm guillotine separated these areas. The light compartment’s dimensions were 30 × 20 × 20 cm, and the walls were made of Plexiglas. The floor of the dark compartment was furnished with conducting wires and connected to a 5 mA, 12 V shock device [ ]. Before the passive avoidance test, the animals were allowed to acclimate to the conditions, and following each test, the cage was cleaned. After resting in the light compartment, a 0.5 mA electric shock was administered to the rat for 3 s via the conducting wire when they entered the dark compartment. After being placed back into the light compartment, the latency time before reentering the dark compartment was recorded. The rats exposed to electrical shocks were returned to their cages within 10 s. This section of the test was called the learning period. Twenty-four hours after the learning period, the rats were returned to the light compartment and the duration before entering the dark compartment was again recorded. This period was called the retention time. 2.6. Biochemical analysis At the end of the experimental process, 1 ml of intra-cardiac blood was collected into tubes during the cardiac perfusion. The samples were centrifuged at 4°C at 2000 rpm for 15 min (Hettich EB 20 centrifuge, Hettich, Tuttlingen, Germany). The serum samples from each rat were stored at −80°C. The serum enzyme activity of GSH, CAT and SOD was measured using a Cayman Kit (Cayman Chemical Company). Additionally, GSH, CAT and SOD enzyme activity was determined at 410 nm, 540 nm and 450 nm, respectively. 2.7. Electrophysiological assessment Under anesthesia (mixture of ketamine HCl 9 mg/kg i.p and 1 mg/kg xylazine i.p.), the cranium of each rat was positioned in a stereotactic device (Harvard Stereotaxic Instruments, Massachusetts, USA), and a 3 cm rostrocaudal incision was made in the scalp. Next, four small holes (each approximately 1 mm in diameter) were drilled 4 mm anterior and posterior to the bregma, and left and right laterally at 3 mm from the midline. Four electrodes were fixed to the skull and isolated with dental cement. After surgery, each animal was allowed to recover for seven days in a separate cage. The basal activity signal from the electrodes was amplified with a BioAmp (ADInstruments, Australia), and transferred to PowerLab 4/SP (ADInstruments Pty Ltd., Castle Hill, Australia). Brain electrical activity was analyzed with LabChart v 7.3.7 software (ADInstruments). The power spectrum of each sample was segmented into six frequency bands: delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4.1–8 Hz), alpha (8.1–15 Hz), beta (16–31 Hz), gamma-1 (32–45 Hz) and gamma-2 (55–100 Hz). All electroencephalographic (EEG) analyses were performed on the first, fifth, tenth and fifteenth days before and after exposure for each group. 2.8. Structural analysis pyramidal cell number in the hippocampus Pyramidal cell numbers were estimated using the optical fractionator technique [ ]. Significant cell loss was observed in the EMF group compared to the other study groups (p < 0.01). Protective effects were evident in that there were no significant differences between the Cont and the EMF + Mel, or between the Cont and the EMF + ω3 in terms of the number of pyramidal cells in the cornu ammonis (CA) CA1 and CA2 regions (p > 0.05). On the other hand, there was no significant difference among the cell numbers for the EMF, the Cont, and the EMF + Mel in terms of the number of pyramidal neurons in the CA3 region. In contrast, a significantly increased cell number was found within the CA3 region in the EMF + ω3 group compared to the other groups (p < 0.01) (Figs. and ). The CE and CV values were within acceptable ranges ( ). 3.2. Granular cell number in the DG In terms of granular cell number, the granular cell number was significantly decreased in the EMF group compared with the Cont group (p < 0.01). Additionally, there was highly significant cell lost in the EMF group compared to EMF + ω3 and EMF + Mel groups (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the EMF + ω3 group showed an increased number of granular cells in comparison to the Cont and the EMF + Mel groups (p < 0.01) (Figs. and ). Evidence for a protective effect was evident in that there was no significant difference between the Cont and the EMF + Mel (p > 0.05). The CE and CV values were within acceptable ranges ( ). 3.3. It was observed that melatonin has a neuroprotective effect on Purkinje cells due to the absence of any difference between the EMF + Mel and the Cont groups. The same neuroprotective effects were seen in the ω3-exposed group, i.e. the EMF + ω3 and the Cont (p > 0.05) (Figs. and ). The CE and CV values were within acceptable ranges ( ). 3.4. Electrophysiological assessment Electroencephalograms (EEGs) were analyzed to determine the changes in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma-1 and gamma-2 bands. Band powers were obtained by 1-min Fast Fourier Transformation (FFT) analysis for representative traces from continuous digital EEG recordings, and then used to calculate the relative band power for each band (percentage of the total power 0.1–50 Hz). Statistical analysis revealed no significant differences between the total power values for the delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma-2 bands among the groups (p > 0.05). There were significant differences between the groups in terms of gamma-1 relative power. Compared to the Cont group, a significant decrease was observed in the EMF group 15 days before exposure and one and five days after EMF exposure (p < 0.05). Discussion Previous studies reported that as a result of EMF exposure to levels comparable to current cell phones, the numbers of hippocampal pyramidal neurons and granule cells in the DG of the EMF group were decreased when compared to the control group [ ]. Terzi et al. [ ] more recently noted that sensitivity to EMF exposure could lead to neurodegenerative disorders as well as cancer and other degenerative chronic illnesses. Furthermore, neuroendocrinological changes may be seen after pronounced EMF exposure and this can cause cognitive effects that cannot easily be monitored in the human population. Despite these important considerations, little is known about the potential structural or functional impacts of EMF, nor of ways to mitigate such impacts through the use of melatonin, polyphenols or other antioxidants. While calcium channels appear to be critical pathways, mechanisms of neurobehavioral and other functional impacts of EMF exposure remain unclear [ ]. Intriguing hypotheses involving the opioid receptor have been elucidated previously. Naloxone is used to block heroin overdoses because of its capacity to interfere with the opioid receptor. Animal studies have found that after EMF stimulation, rodents previously conditioned to respond for a food reward will not seek that food reward when injected with naloxone. Thus, indicating that EMF can have a direct physiological impact on addictive behaviors [ ]. The hippocampus is critical for controlling some behavioral and cognitive functions, which includes storing and retaining information during and after learning. According to Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM), the most popular standard for mobile phones is 900 MHz [ ]. Thus, 900-MHz wave frequencies were chosen for this study. Harmful environmental conditions may deeply affect neurogenesis in the brain that occurs during the prenatal period, and such conditions may have increased neurobiological or concurrent behavioral defects [ ]. Others have also previously shown that weakly powered digital EMF can have both structural and functional impacts on the brain and behavior. Odaci et al. reported a decrease in the number of granule neurons in the DG of rats exposed to 900 MHz EMF during the prenatal period when compared with the control group [ ]. Furthermore, a great number of morphological deteriorations have been shown to occur in addition to a decrease in cell number [ ]. Using a design similar to this study, Bas et al. found that four week old rats which had been prenatally exposed to 900 MHz EMF experienced a decrease in the total number of pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus when compared with controls [ ]. In their study, Sonmez et al. reported that no change occurred in the number of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum of adult female rats, which had been exposed, to an hour of EMF for 28 days; however, there was an obvious decrease in the Purkinje numbers when compared with the control group and the sham group [ ]. In another study by Bas et al., researchers found a significant decrease in the pyramidal neuron numbers in the hippocampus of adult females exposed to an hour of EMF daily for a period of 28 days [ ] as compared with sham and other controls. Lai and Singh have reported that exposure to radiofrequency waves induced DNA fragmentation in rat brain cells [ ]. In line with this finding, Robison et al. also observed that EMF exposure in HL-60 and HL-60R cells is associated with decreased DNA repair rates [ ]. In considering pathological processes that occur in biological systems due to EMF exposure, ROS and the action of free radicals in the cells appears critical. Lipids also play a role in intercellular signal transmission since they are critical to multiple unsaturated fatty acids and amino acids membrane structure that are easily damaged by ROS. When hydrogen is removed from unsaturated chains in the membrane, carbon radicals form and react with oxygen to produce highly reactive and unstable peroxyl radicals. Some antioxidant enzymes have the capacity to scavenge free radicals and provide chemoprotection. Low levels of these enzymes in the brain and high levels of naturally protective fatty acids that can be easily oxidized in neuron membranes are proof of the brain’s predisposition for oxidative damage [ ]. Due to the rapid cellular traffic between neuronal membranes, brain tissue is quite sensitive to oxidative stress. When the rate of ROS increases in an organism, calcium is released and becomes free. This increase in free calcium causes membrane structure and enzyme activities to deteriorate; as a result, nitric oxide radical formation is increased, resulting in concomitant cell damage and can directly or indirectly induce apoptosis [ ]. Morphologically, EMF-exposed cells are characterized by a decrease in cell volume, deterioration in membrane integrity, and nuclear fragmentation. Studies have confirmed the oxidative damage of a great number of apoptotic proteins, such as caspase [ ]. Additionally, İkinci et al. reported that continuous exposure to 900 MHz EMF can affect the development of the human fetus spinal cord in the gestational period. They observed histopathological changes in the spinal cord exposed to EMF such as vacuolization, atrophy, and thickening. They also found significant changes in MDA, SOD and CAT levels of exposed spinal cord tissues [ ] It is known that the cerebellum is critically involved in learning, balance, impulse control, memory and the formation of synapses. Purkinje cells form many synapses with the dendrites of granule cells. A number of studies have reported that EMF affects the number of granule cell numbers in the cerebellum and have implicated changes in the DNA structure as the underlying cause [ ]. Investigations of Martin Pall (ref) have shown that EMF alters the activity of calcium channels and hypothesized that this affects membrane conductivity. Thus, changes in voltage may lead to granule cells necrosis or apoptosis [ ]. Yet other investigators have reported no such results regarding a decrease or an increase in the number of granule cells due to non-ionizing radiation. In that regard, our study did not find a statistically significant difference between the EMF-exposed and other treatment arms in terms of the number of granule cells in the cerebellum [ ]. We obtained similar results when we compared the EMF and control groups of our young adult rats. Clearly, the impact on granular cell formation of the hippocampus is a topic that merits further investigations with special attention to be paid to the age of exposure. It is noteworthy that oxidative stress-induced loss, which was seen in the cerebellar granule cells exposed during the prenatal period, was not observed in those exposed as adult rats. This situation raises the question of whether there are critical windows of exposure during which prenatal exposure can affect cerebellar development, but adult exposures have no such impact. EMF exposure does not only result in a loss of granular cells, but also definitely influences granule cell migration [ ]. Molecular studies that include the prenatal period should therefore be conducted to clarify whether critical periods of vulnerability exist for EMF as they do for other well-known pollutants such as lead or other heavy metals. Mel, which is secreted from the pineal gland, is a direct radical scavenger and antioxidant [ ]. Since it is highly lipophilic, Mel can be easily transferred to all tissues. Thus, studies have shown that it can decrease the oxidative stress in the central nervous system [ ]. Due to this characteristic, it can easily enter all cellular components and offer a neuroprotective effect. Another study showed that Mel significantly decreased brain damage caused by ischemic reperfusion. Thus, the antioxidant efficiency of Mel and its free radical scavenging activities are undeniable [ ]. A study by Sutcu et al. found that in addition to the anticancer and antioxidant activity of Mel, it also increased the NMDA (N-methyl- D -aspartic acid) receptor activity in the hippocampus [ ]. In addition to showing the structurally protective effects of Mel and ω3, our work also demonstrates the protective effects of ω3 and Mel after EMF exposure on functional outcomes such as learning and memory through the results of the passive avoidance tests. Animals exposed to their neuroprotective agents in addition to EMF experienced no decrease in performance as compared to those with EMF exposure alone. In general, Mel is initially given exogenously, and then physiological Mel release continued [ ]. The other protective compound that we evaluated here is ω3–a fatty acid that has become a subject of a great number of studies, especially due to its protective effects on the cardiovascular system. Although the present study indicates a protective effect of ω3 after EMF exposure, it will be important to explore further studies i.e. electron microscopic, immunohistochemical and biochemical studies. This enzyme is especially higher in the kidney, liver, and erythrocytes than in other organs [ ]. An increased amount of SOD, CAT, and GSH in the hippocampal tissues exposed to EMF can be seen in other studies [ ]. In addition, high CAT and GSH activities in the EMF + Mel and EMF groups may indicate that the level of free radicals is very high, stimulating high amounts of antioxidant enzymes. Our study also found that a varying duration of a 900-MHz EMF application resulted in no significant difference in most of the EEG waves, with the notable exception of the gamma-1 band; other bands remained unchanged in terms of relative power in response to magnetic field application. The gamma band of the mammalian brain encompasses the fastest frequencies [ ] and is generally related to cross-modal sensory processing and short-term memory matching of recognized objects, sounds, or sensations. In this regard, a decrease in gamma bands can be interpreted as a sign of cognitive decline [ ]. We find an important and significant decline in the EMF exposed groups in general, especially after 15 days of regular applications. Interestingly, it appears that both Mel and ω3 applications block these effects so that results are comparable to those of the Cont group. Specific attention must be also directed to the changes in faster EEG bands in order to evaluate brain effects of such EMF exposure. In addition, many studies have shown a cell loss in the hippocampus, DG, and cerebellum because of being exposed to a 900 MHz EMF for an hour every day for 15 days of period [ ]. Our study has importantly found neuroprotective effects of Mel and ω3 based on the antioxidant defense system as evidenced through histological and biochemical analyses. Thus, consistent with a number of previous investigations our study finds that EMF from mobile phones induces degenerative effects on neurons of critical components of the brain and that Mel and ω3 separately provide important neuroprotective effects against these damaging impacts through increasing antioxidants. chunks.content: Introduction Polonium-210 ( 210 Po) is a natural radionuclide which decays to 206 Pb, emitting alpha particles with energy of 5.3044 (100%) and 4.5166 MeV (0.00122%) [ ]. The half-life of 210 Po is 138.376 days [ ], which corresponds to a specific activity of 1.66 × 10 14 Bq g −1 . High amounts of pure 210 Po activity can be produced by three ways: the activation of 209 Bi (natural abundance 100%) with thermal neutrons (cross section σ = 0.034 barn), the separation from 222 Rn daughter nuclides emanated from 226 Ra, and the separation from Pb–Bi alloy coolants of some fast neutron reactors. 210 Po is a decay daughter of 210 Pb in 238 U decay chain of the uranium series; it occurs in the uranium ores and exists ubiquitously in the environment. According to the United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation (UNSCEAR) [ ], the concentration of 210 Po in air is reported to be from 10 to 80 μBq m −3 with a reference value of 50 μBq m −3 ; the annual intake of the public ranges from 18 Bq in South America to 220 Bq in Asia with a reference value of 58 Bq. Through inhalation and diet 210 Po is accumulated in the human body, its concentration in human tissues is 200 mBq kg −1 in lungs, 600 mBq kg −1 in liver, 600 mBq kg −1 in kidneys, 100 mBq kg −1 in muscle and other tissues, and 2,400 mBq kg −1 in bone. However, these body contents are reference values, they vary between individuals. The presence of 210 Po in tobacco greatly increases the intake of this radionuclide by smokers. Recently, Desideri et al. [ ] reported that in Italy smokers who smoke 20 cigarettes per day inhale, on average, 79.5 mBq of 210 Po daily; those smokers concomitantly inhale the same amount of radioactivity from 210 Pb. The measured 210 Po concentration in lung parenchyma of smokers is about three times that of non-smokers [ ]. Hill reported a higher content of 210 Po in kidneys, liver, lungs, and gonads for smokers compared to non-smokers [ ]. With regard to daily excretion, Glöbel et al. [ ] reported in 1966 the measurements in one German subject to be in the range of 40.7–351.5 mBq in feces and 2.2–37 mBq in urine. Naumann et al. [ ] reported daily urinary excretion ranging from 2.8 (detection limit of 2 mBq l −1 with urinary excretion of 1.4 l d −1 ) to 9.9 mBq d −1 in Berlin area. Dalheimer et al. [ ] recently reported a daily urinary excretion median value of 3.5 mBq d −1 for non-smokers and 6.6 mBq d −1 for smokers. In Brazil, the reported values of 210 Po excretion in urine were 5.2 mBq l −1 for non-smokers and 9.8 mBq l −1 for smokers [ , ]. In Saudi Arabia, the measured values range from 1.5 to 10 mBq l −1 for non-smokers and 3.3 to 15.9 mBq l −1 for smokers [ ]. According to the model recommended by the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP), about 10–50% of ingested 210 Po is absorbed by the intestine and flows into the bloodstream and mostly deposits in the liver, kidneys, spleen, red bone marrow and other tissues [ ]. To distinguish between ingestion of the organic and inorganic forms of polonium, ICRP recommended an f 1 value of 0.1 for workers and 0.5 for members of the public [ ]. For intake by inhalation, ICRP recommended an f 1 value of 0.1 for workers and members of the public inhaling the material of Type F (fast absorption into blood) and M (moderate absorption into blood) [ , ], an f 1 value of 0.01 was used for members of the public inhaling the material of Type S (slow absorption into blood) [ ]. The effective dose coefficients of 210 Po for adult members of the public recommended by ICRP are 1.2 × 10 −6 Sv Bq −1 for ingestion calculated with an f 1 value of 0.5, and 3.3 × 10 −6 Sv Bq −1 for inhalation assuming a material of Type M with an f 1 value of 0.1 [ ]. As reported in the media, Mr. Alexander Litvinenko died 23 days (the 23rd of November 2006 was included) after he was possibly poisoned by 210 Po. In this context, the organ absorbed doses in the days following, say from days 1 to 30, after acute intake of 210 Po are important for intake lethal dose estimation. The equivalent dose and effective dose coefficients are needed for the effective dose and the risk assessments of other probably contaminated members of the public. In this context, the organ absorbed doses in the days following, say from days 1 to 30, after acute intake of 210 Po are important for intake lethal dose estimation. The equivalent dose and effective dose coefficients are needed for the effective dose and the risk assessments of other probably contaminated members of the public. In the present work, the daily urinary and fecal excretions, the time-dependence of the equivalent dose and the effective dose from 1 to 1,000 days after acute ingestion and inhalation of 1 Bq of 210 Po were calculated using the biokinetic model for polonium recommended by ICRP [ ] and the model recently developed by Leggett and Eckerman (L&E) [ ]. These modeled excretions and dose coefficients can be used for the estimate of intake and the risk assessment, provided that the 210 Po urinary or other excreta data are available from the people who were potentially contaminated in this 210 Po accident. The GSF Radioanalytical Laboratory measured urine samples of seven German subjects who were suspected to have been exposed to traces of 210 Po in the aftermath of the poisoning of Mr. Litvinenko. Those measured results and the calculated conversion factors of the daily urinary excretion to effective dose are applied to assess the effective dose for those persons. In order to estimate the possible intake of 210 Po and organ dose for Mr. Litvinenko, the mean organ absorbed dose was calculated applying the two above-mentioned models. The results obtained using ICRP and L&E models are compared and critically discussed. Materials and methods Experimental measurement of urinary excretion of <sup>210</sup>Po Seven persons (5 male and 2 female) aged from 23 to 48 years from Germany provided their 24-h-urine samples in December 2006. Among those persons only one was a smoker. Information on the suspected day of exposure to 210 Po was also acquired. Samples were measured between 6 and 12 days after the possible exposure. The complete 24-h-urine samples were transferred into appropriate glass beakers. The sampling containers were washed twice with 20 ml 9 M HCl. The washing solutions were added to the samples. About 160 mBq 208 Po yield tracer and 1 g ascorbic acid per liter urine were added. Polonium was deposited onto copper discs (20 h, 20°C). The urine was discarded and the discs were rinsed with water and isopropanole. The polonium isotopes were determined by alpha spectrometry with Canberra PIPS detectors in vacuum chambers. The spectra were evaluated with Eurisys Interwinner Software. The analytical procedure was last validated by participating in the IAEA proficiency test IAEA-CU-2007-09 on the determination of 210 Po in water. Biokinetic model of <sup>210</sup>Po The ICRP and L&E systemic biokinetic models of polonium [ , ], coupled with the gastrointestinal tract model of ICRP Publication 30 [ ] and the respiratory tract model of ICRP Publication 66 [ ], were used to calculate the retentions of 210 Po in organs or tissues after incorporation. In the ICRP model, a fraction of 30, 10, 5, 10, and 45% of polonium entering into the systemic circulation is deposited in the liver, kidneys, spleen, red marrow and the rest of the body, respectively. It is retained in those organs with a half-life of 50 days. A ratio of 1:2 between the urinary and fecal excretions is assumed for systemic polonium [ ]. Recently, an improved, physiologically realistic systemic biokinetic model for polonium in humans was constructed by Leggett and Eckerman based on the data identified to most likely represent the typical behavior of polonium in laboratory animals and human subjects [ ]. In contrast to the current ICRP model, the new proposed model enables one to predict the excretion of polonium in human hair and sweat. In addition, a compartment representing the bone surface was integrated into the model of polonium. The urinary excretion pathway is more physiologically realistic than the current ICRP model. Therefore, the new model is expected to provide a more reliable estimation of the intake and the effective dose from the measured urinary excretion data. Dose calculation of <sup>210</sup>Po after ingestion and inhalation The average organ absorbed dose, D T , in an organ or a tissue T , due to nuclear transformations, U S , of a radionuclide in various source organs S , is calculated applying the methodology developed by the Medical Internal Radiation Dose (MIRD) Committee [ ]: where is the time-integrated, or cumulated activity, and is equal to the number of transformations U S in S ; S ( T ← S ) is the absorbed dose in T per unit cumulated activity in S . The equivalent dose, H T , is given by summing the product of U S and the specific effective energy [SEE( T ← S )] over all source organs, S [ ]. In the values of the specific effective energy each type of radiation is weighted by a given radiation weighting factor, which accounts for the different effectiveness in inducing late effects. The U S of the radionuclide in the source organ or tissue was obtained by integrating the retention function, which was modeled by the SAAM II program (University of Washington, Seattle, WA). The values of S ( T ← S ) and SEE( T ← S ) were calculated by using the SEECAL program [ ]. The effective dose, E , was calculated by the sum of the product of the equivalent dose, H T and the corresponding tissue weighting factor, w T , over 12 organs and tissues ( T ) and the product between the equivalent dose of the so called remainder tissue, H rem , and its weighting factor, w rem [ , ]. The equivalent dose of the colon, H colon , was calculated as 0.57 × H ULI + 0.43 × H LLI , where H ULI and H LLI are the equivalent doses in the walls of the upper large intestine (ULI) and the lower large intestine (LLI), respectively [ ]. The dose of thymus is taken as a surrogate for the oesophagus, in absence of a dosimetric model for the oesophagus [ ]. For the lungs, the apportionment factors for target cells in different lung regions recommended by ICRP were used [ ]. Secondly, the time-dependent organ equivalent dose, effective dose, organ absorbed dose and daily excretion in urine and in feces, in hair and sweat after acute ingestion and inhalation of 210 Po are shown. The average values of body content and daily excretion of 210 Po for the normal unexposed public are estimated. Finally, the effective doses for the possibly contaminated seven subjects are predicted. The amount of 210 Po Mr. Litvinenko probably ingested are estimated and discussed based on different assumptions. Because 210 Po is an alpha emitter (negligible contribution to dose from gamma ray), the organ absorbed doses are 20 times smaller than the corresponding values of the organ equivalent dose since a radiation weighting factor of 20 for alpha particles is applied in calculating the organ equivalent dose. The highest organ absorbed doses are in the kidneys after intake for ingestion, and in the lungs after inhalation. Doses to members of the public are generally higher than for workers; the L&E model gives lower estimates than the ICRP model. The dose absorbed by the red marrow per unit ingestion (inhalation), calculated using the ICRP model for members of the public, is 1.5 × 10 −3 (1.4 × 10 −4 ) Gy MBq −1 at 1 day after incorporation, 2.2 × 10 −2 (2.1 × 10 −3 ) Gy MBq −1 at 10 days, 5.7 × 10 −2 (6.0 × 10 −3 ) Gy MBq −1 at 30 days, and 1.1 × 10 −1 (1.5 × 10 −2 ) Gy MBq −1 at 100 days, respectively. <sup>210</sup>Po daily excretion in urine and in feces after acute intake The predicted daily excretions in urine and in feces, by using both models, are shown in Fig. . However, it is not obvious to assess the intake and level of 210 Po in the body from hair measurements because their results are highly dependent on modality of sample collection and because the model does not discriminate between excretion into sweat and hair. In the first few days after incorporation, the amount of 210 Po excreted in urine is markedly higher than that in hair and sweat (of a factor up to 25 times). They are tabulated in Table . In the earlier days, the factor E/U is larger than E’/U, however, after 300 days from intake, those two factors reach the same value. Applying the ICRP model for members of the public, the content of 210 Po in human body is predicted to be about 1.1 Bq. It is estimated that about 4 mBq in urine and 0.15 Bq in feces could be found daily. These results are in excellent agreement with the experimental values reported in the literature [ – , , ]. documents.title: ICRP Publication 139 occupational radiological protection in interventional procedures

chunks.content: Introduction The increasing volume and complexity of diagnostic and interventional cardiovascular (CV) procedures have led to a progressive rise in exposure to ionizing radiation (IR) in cardiac catheterization laboratories (Cath Labs). , This trend has relevant implications not only for patients, who may accumulate low-dose exposure across multiple, technically demanding procedures, but also for healthcare professionals, who are repeatedly exposed over the course of their careers. , Radiation protection has therefore become an integral component of contemporary cardiovascular care. , This document builds on the 2023 ANMCO Position Paper focused on radiological protection in interventional cardiology and provides an updated, broader perspective on occupational risk in Cath Labs. While the previous document primarily addressed radiation safety issues, this paper adopts a broader perspective on occupational risk in the Cath Labs, including updated evidence and additional dimensions of professional exposure. Since 2023, developments in radiation biology, molecular epidemiology, and large-scale cohort analysis have substantially improved our understanding of the biological effects of chronic low-dose radiation exposure. These developments have expanded the focus beyond oncological risk, drawing attention to potential cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and even reproductive sequelae that may emerge with prolonged exposure ( ). , , At the same time, there is a growing awareness of occupational risks unrelated to radiation, including musculoskeletal disorders associated with prolonged use of radiation protection equipment, exposure to blood-borne pathogens such as hepatitis B and C viruses and human immunodeficiency virus, and finally, the psychological stress inherent to high-intensity procedures have highlighted the intrinsically multidimensional risk profile of the cardiac Cath Lab environment. Advances in technology further justify this broader perspective. Modern Cath Labs now have access to advanced shielding systems, structured dose-optimization strategies, and imaging innovations that substantially reduce exposure. Moreover, the increasing adoption of non-fluoroscopic approaches in cardiac electrophysiology (EP) and selected interventional procedures, including electro-anatomical mapping systems and ultrasound-guided techniques, supports a gradual transition towards radiation-sparing and, in selected settings, potentially radiation-free workflows. For these reasons, the present document should not be interpreted as simply an update to the 2023 ANMCO Position Paper. Rather, it represents a broader and more articulated framework, developed in response to evolving evidence and aimed at extending both the scientific depth and the conceptual reach of the original document. The aim of this document is to provide a comprehensive, evidence-informed appraisal of occupational hazards in the cardiac Cath Labs, integrating data through 2026 and encouraging a renewed, more accountable culture of safety within interventional cardiology. By bringing together scientific evidence, technological progress, structured education, and principles of clinical governance, it seeks to reinforce protection standards while safeguarding the long-term sustainability of contemporary interventional CV practice. Occupational hazards in the cardiac catheterization laboratory Working in the cardiac Cath Labs exposes healthcare professionals to a range of occupational hazards that may be broadly grouped into four principal domains: IR exposure; musculoskeletal strain associated with prolonged use of protective equipment; occupational exposure to blood and other body fluids; and psychological stress related to sustained procedural intensity and workload ( ). Radiation exposure in patients and staff Radiation exposure remains a major concern in cardiac cath labs, affecting not only patients but also the healthcare professionals involved in procedural care. The United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation (UNSCEAR) defines the low-dose and low-dose rate for radiation protection as <100 milliSievert (mSv) and < 6 mSv/h, respectively. The main difference between interventional cardiologists and patients exposed to radiation from fluoroscopy procedures is not primarily determined by the total dose received (100–200 mSv), but the dose rate, typically 100–1000 mSv/h for patients and 100–1000 microSievert/h (low-dose rate) for medical workers. Patient exposure, typically expressed as effective dose, varies substantially according to procedural complexity, ranging from fractions of an mSv to several hundred mSv. To facilitate clinical interpretation, radiation doses are often compared with standard postero-anterior chest X-rays (CXRs). For example, simple procedures (e.g. pacemaker implantation): ∼0.5 mSv (equivalent to 25 CXRs); common procedures (e.g. percutaneous coronary intervention): 15 mSv (750 CXRs), but up to 100 mSv (5000 CXRs) for dilation of chronic total occlusion; complex interventions (e.g. thoracic aortic repair): up to 200 mSv (∼10 000 CXRs) (2,3); advanced structural heart procedures (e.g. transcatheter valve interventions): in some institutions, 29% of cases exceed 2 Sv (100 000 CXRs). An interventional cardiologist performing 1000 procedures as the primary operator accumulates a dose comparable to a single-patient exposure. Health risks associated with occupational radiation exposure Cancer risk Radiation-induced cancer represents the primary stochastic risk for Cath Labs’ staff, with a probability that increases proportionally with the cumulative dose. A cumulative dose of 100 mSv (equivalent to 5000 CXRs) corresponds to an excess cancer risk of 1.0–1.3% (fatal and non-fatal combined), with evidence matured in the last 20 years increasing the previous risk estimates of Biological Effects of Ionising Radiation Committee VII Committee, 2006, for the same dose exposure, up to 30%. , The head and neck are particularly vulnerable anatomical regions, with left-sided cranial exposure approximately two-fold higher than right-sided exposure, largely reflecting operator positioning relative to the X-ray source. This asymmetric pattern has been linked in observational reports to a higher incidence of left-sided brain tumours, including glioblastoma, meningioma, and neurinoma, although causality remains a matter of ongoing investigation ; skin, with unprotected areas (especially left-sided) showing elevated rates of basal cell carcinoma ; lung and haematological cancers, with excess risks observed for lung cancer, leukaemia (except chronic lymphocytic leukaemia), and lymphoma. Findings from traditional epidemiological approaches can be meaningfully complemented by molecular epidemiology, which integrates intermediate biomarkers of biological effects and early predictors of long-term cancer risk. From a conceptual standpoint, this strategy resembles using carotid plaque assessment by vascular ultrasound to identify subclinical disease and improve the prediction of subsequent cardiovascular events in asymptomatic populations. In the oncological setting, relevant biomarkers include chromosomal aberrations, such as dicentrics and micronuclei in lymphocytes, which reflect genomic instability and are associated with an elevated long-term cancer risk. This effect is further amplified by factors such as smoking, a well-established mutagen, or polymorphisms in DNA repair genes that impair their function. Cardiovascular disease Recent evidence suggests that low-dose IR may accelerate atherosclerosis, with cardiovascular risks potentially comparable to those of cancer, thereby challenging the traditional cancer-centred focus of radiation protection. Meta-analysis data from a study of 400 000 workers demonstrated dose-dependent increases in ischaemic heart disease, stroke, and overall cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality. A cumulative dose of 100 mSv (equivalent to 5000 CXRs) corresponds to an excess risk of CVD around 1.0% (fatal and non-fatal events combined). , In the context of atherosclerosis, epidemiological observations have been supported by molecular epidemiological findings showing that interventional cardiologists have shorter leukocyte telomere length, a recognized marker of accelerated vascular ageing. The fundamental mechanism underlying the induction of atherosclerotic CVD is low-grade inflammation that triggers DNA damage and endothelial dysfunction. , Individuals with clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential face disproportionately elevated risks. Neurodegenerative disease Recent evidence has raised concern regarding a potential association between IR exposure and neurodegenerative disorders. Reproductive health In males, doses as low as 150 mSv reduce sperm counts; 300 mSv causes transient azoospermia. Exposed workers exhibit poor motility, DNA fragmentation, hypermethylation, and overall reduced sperm quality. The molecular epidemiology approach shows a greater Y chromosome instability. , An increased copy number variation within the azoospermia factor c (AZFc) region of the Y chromosome has been recognized as a genomic marker associated with impaired spermatogenesis and male infertility. In men, the most vulnerable period for radiation-related reproductive effects is the approximately 90 days preceding conception, corresponding to the full spermatogenic cycle. During this interval, germ cells progress from relatively radio-resistant spermatogonia to highly radiosensitive mature spermatozoa, which lack cytoplasm and intrinsic cellular defence mechanisms against radiation-induced damage. Concerns about foetal irradiation and its potential health effects remain a major issue for women pursuing careers in invasive cardiology. , The lack of robust data in this field is further evidenced by disparate safety standards for foetal protection in pregnant workers. In contrast, most European countries prioritize the safety of the unborn child, enforcing a stricter limit of < 1 mSv and requiring pregnant women to leave the cardiac Cath Labs once pregnancy is confirmed. Although quantifying exact risks remains challenging, IR exposure is associated with an increased likelihood of miscarriage, small-for-gestational-age newborns, childhood leukaemia, and congenital malformations. , Paternal exposure to IR during the 3 months preceding conception has been associated with more than a three-fold increase in the risk of sporadic bilateral retinoblastoma, a condition typically arising from a de novo germline mutation of the RB1 (retinoblastoma-1) gene. Changes in DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs are viable mechanistic candidates for the non-genetic transfer of paternal environmental information from maturing germ cells to zygotes. Although the issue of the transgenerational effects of low-dose radiation exposure remains unsettled, it is now established that not only mothers but also fathers occupationally exposed to high levels of carcinogenic substances may endanger not only themselves but also their children. Ocular complications Approximately one in two interventional cardiologists develop posterior subcapsular cataracts, largely attributable to chronic, insufficiently shielded ocular exposure. This elevated prevalence can be explained by several factors. First, the operator’s eyes are directly exposed to scattered X-rays generated during fluoroscopic procedures. In the absence of appropriate leaded eye protection, the crystalline lens may receive an entrance dose of several hundred microSieverts per coronary angiography session, with cumulative exposure over time reaching clinically relevant thresholds. A second, and largely preventable, factor is the inconsistent use of appropriate leaded eyewear among operators. Third, historical occupational dose limits for the lens were set at levels now considered insufficiently protective, potentially allowing cumulative exposures that could induce lens damage before the adequate awareness of risk was established. On 21 April 2011, the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) revised its recommendations for occupational exposure to the eye lens, lowering the annual dose limit from 150 mSv to 20 mSv, averaged over a 5-year period, with the additional constraint that no single year should exceed 50 mSv. Current evidence suggests that a clear threshold dose for radiation-induced cataract cannot be reliably defined. Although lens opacities have traditionally been regarded as a prototypical tissue reaction (formerly termed deterministic or non-stochastic) with an assumed threshold above 0.5 Sv, more recent data indicate that lens damage may occur at substantially lower doses ( ). Moreover, the risk per unit dose appears to be proportionally greater at low cumulative doses and low dose rates, challenging earlier radiobiological assumptions. The likely mechanism of radiation-induced cataract is that the lens epithelium, especially in the posterior pole, is very sensitive to IR. Unlike other tissues, the lens has no cell turnover: once lens epithelial cells are damaged, the effect accumulates. Radiation damages DNA and proteins, leading to abnormal migration and differentiation of the lens epithelial cells beneath the capsule, where they migrate and clump abnormally. Radiation-independent risks: orthopaedic hazards from protective gear Although radiation shielding remains indispensable for exposure control, the prolonged use of conventional lead aprons introduces distinct occupational hazards. These predominantly orthopaedic and, in some cases, neurological disorders are not radiation-related but arise from the chronic mechanical load imposed by heavy protective garments. The risk is further amplified by sustained static postures, repetitive movements, and suboptimal ergonomics that characterize daily practice in the Cath Labs. Standard lead aprons (0.25–0.50 mm Pb-equivalent) weigh 5–10 kg, placing sustained stress on the spine and joints. Due to weight and strain, 50% of interventional cardiologists report cervical/lumbar pain, hip/knee degeneration, or spinal damage. Severe cases progress to spinal cord compression, paralysis, or career-ending disability. In addition, protective gear has a documented risk of surface toxicity. Thyroid collars show 80% contamination with lead dust (vs. 40% in aprons) due to frequent folding and sweat exposure , , Biomonitoring analyses indicate that personnel working in Cath Labs have hair lead concentrations approximately three-fold higher than those of non-exposed healthcare workers, suggesting chronic environmental and occupational exposure in interventional settings. No safe threshold exists for lead exposure, raising concerns about chronic toxicity. Traditional lead shielding is life-saving, but its weight, toxicity, and recycling challenges make it a double-edged sword, potentially overcome by innovative, effective shielding materials such as lead-free multilayered polymer composites and non-lead nanocomposite shields. Using several high-density, high-atomic-number elements, such as bismuth, barium, gadolinium, and tungsten, significantly enhances the shielding ability of composites. Infectious hazards in the cath lab: blood-borne pathogens and prevention strategies Interventional cardiology personnel are at measurable risk of exposure to blood-borne pathogens, with percutaneous injuries posing a significant occupational hazard. Needlestick events have been reported in approximately 0.6% of vascular procedures, while glove perforation rates approach 1% per intervention. Over the course of their professional careers, nearly 80% of interventional cardiologists report at least one percutaneous injury, and more than one-third report having sustained a sharp-related injury within the previous year. The three most concerning bloodborne pathogens and their transmission rates following percutaneous exposure are hepatitis B virus, with a 30% transmission risk and the highest infectivity, but vaccine-preventable; hepatitis C virus, with 1.9% transmission risk and no vaccine available; and human immunodeficiency virus, with the lowest (0.3%) transmission risk but the most feared consequence. Psychological distress and burnout in interventional cardiology Interventional cardiology offers unique professional satisfactions, with high reward: life-saving interventions with immediate patient impact; rapid technological evolution (e.g. robotic interventions); team-based achievements with specialized staff; financial compensation, since the average U.S. interventional cardiologist earns $700 K/year, 50% higher than non-invasive cardiologists. Yet, these rewards come at a high psychological cost, with 70% of practitioners experiencing burnout and a gender disparity; 65% of female interventionalists report burnout vs. 48% of males. Several structural and organizational factors contribute to this risk profile, including sustained workload intensity, often averaging approximately 63 working hours per week, continuous 24/7 on-call responsibilities, and cumulative decision fatigue associated with managing complex, time-critical procedures. Additional environmental and occupational stressors may further compound this burden. These include persistent radiation-related concerns, together with the potential neurobiological effects of chronic low-dose exposure that may increase susceptibility to mood disturbances, physical strain from prolonged standing and the use of heavy lead aprons, and the emotional impact of adverse clinical outcomes. Notably, up to 42% of operators report features consistent with ‘compassion fatigue’, and 58% describe a sense of social isolation despite maintaining personal relationships. After leaving the cardiac Cath Labs, professional pressures persist. Interventional cardiologists remain subject to productivity-driven performance audits, encounter a malpractice litigation risk estimated to be about twice that of colleagues in general cardiology, and face a considerable administrative workload, with nearly 33% of their time devoted to documentation and related non-clinical tasks. These sustained pressures have tangible consequences on physical and psychological well-being, as well as on personal and social relationships. Reported divorce rates are approximately twice those observed in the general population, the risk of depression is up to four-fold higher, and sleep disorders affect nearly 61% of practitioners. Available data also indicate that younger, unmarried women cardiologists may be particularly susceptible to burnout. A culture in which excessive radiation exposure is tacitly accepted still persists in some settings. This is driven in part by limited formal training in radiation biology among cardiologists, the insidious and delayed nature of chronic exposure effects, which reduces the perception of immediate risk, and financial constraints that may hinder the timely adoption of safer technologies and protective systems. There are now clear cultural, technological, and organizational conditions that make it possible to substantially reduce occupational risk within the cardiac Cath Labs. With robotic-assisted interventions, operators achieve a 97% dose reduction in percutaneous coronary intervention, with precision enhancement and sub-millimetre catheter control. Advanced, non-fluoroscopic imaging modalities reduce radiation exposure by 85% to 95% with intracardiac echocardiography or magnetic navigation, achieving near-zero fluoroscopy in electrophysiology studies. New Food and Drug Administration-cleared protection systems allow a > 90% dose reduction with a setup time of 3 to 6 min. New nanoparticle-based shields are lead-free and 40% lighter while providing the same level of protection. All these changes have a cost in terms of investment and in the institution's and the operators’ expertise. Nevertheless, the net gain is extraordinary when balanced against the reduced long-term risk of operators and patients. In addition, a 90% reduction in radiation exposure can be achieved without any investment, simply by providing dedicated radioprotection courses for operators, who are made aware of the risks of radiation exposure and how to minimize the damage. , It is important to optimize the fluoroscopy time, and even more important to minimize the cine-time, since during the actual recording (‘cine’) sequences, the patient and the operator are exposed to a 10 times higher rate of radiation than during standard fluoroscopy. ‘Live’ Fluoroscopy is like using a handheld camcorder to film behind-the-scenes footage all day. The camera is on for a long time, but it is in a low-quality, efficient mode. ‘Cine’ Acquisition is like rolling the expensive, Hollywood-quality IMAX (Image Maximum) high-resolution camera for the crucial scenes. This camera uses blindingly bright lights and consumes massive amounts of energy, but you only use it for short, critical takes. The total dose is a product of both the high-dose-rate recordings and the long cumulative time of low-dose-rate fluoroscopy. This is why complex interventions like percutaneous coronary interventions are among the highest-dose procedures in radiology. Conclusion: from complacency to vigilance—a new era of radiation safety The message from the data is clear: chronic occupational radiation exposure in interventional cardiology is associated with meaningful long-term risks, affecting not only individuals but potentially entire generations of operators. This calls for a change in attitude. Exposure should no longer be passively accepted as part of the job but addressed with the same rigour applied to patient outcomes and procedural quality. Professional responsibility includes protecting those who deliver care. In this context, Ted Diethrich stands as a relevant example. A pioneer of hybrid revascularization techniques, he was also among the early voices emphasizing the importance of radiation safety and occupational awareness in the cardiac catheterization laboratory, reminding the community that innovation and protection must progress together. For a long time, many operators worked under the quiet assumption that serious harm would not happen to them. The effects of chronic exposure were distant, abstract, and easy to underestimate. With the passing of years, however, the clinical consequences became harder to ignore. Ted Diethrich later developed bilateral cataracts and significant carotid atherosclerotic disease, and in 2012, he was diagnosed with a brain oligodendroglioma. He spoke publicly about his condition, linking it to decades of occupational radiation exposure and urging colleagues to take protection seriously. Towards the end of his life, having suffered from what he thought was radiation-induced illness, he issued a powerful warning to his colleagues: ‘ When we started doing these procedures, nobody questioned what we did. The last thing I was thinking about was how much radiation I am exposed to. Being a doctor, my whole motive was to help the patient get well. I didn’t think about the hazardous conditions’. I felt indestructible. Obviously, I didn’t know what I was talking about’. Concrete change does not require complex reforms; it can begin with deliberate, everyday choices. Consistent use of personal dosimetry, rigorous application of available shielding, and strict adherence to clinical appropriateness are fundamental. Radiation output should be kept as low as reasonably achievable by limiting fluoroscopy and cine acquisition to what is truly necessary. At the institutional level, commitment to investing in advanced dose-reduction systems and more ergonomic protective technologies is essential. In parallel, the progressive integration of non-ionizing imaging modalities offers a realistic path towards reducing cumulative exposure. Ultimately, safeguarding operator health is not secondary to patient care, it is part of it. A mature safety culture recognizes that excellence in interventional cardiology encompasses both procedural success and long-term professional sustainability. Protecting ourselves and our teams ensures we can continue to provide high-quality care throughout our careers. Let this serve as a clear call to action—no more preventable harm. Each time we step into the cardiac catheterization laboratory, we should recall the experience of Ted Diethrich, a pioneer and leading figure in modern cardiology, and allow that memory to guide our conduct and our commitment to safety. Several practical steps can be implemented without delay in routine practice. First, personal dosimeters should be worn consistently, and exposure levels should be periodically reviewed. Second, all available shielding devices and protective equipment should be used appropriately and systematically. Third, examinations lacking clear clinical indication should be avoided. Fourth, radiation delivery must be optimized by limiting fluoroscopy time and, in particular, reducing cine acquisition to what is strictly necessary. Fifth, institutions should be encouraged to invest in advanced dose-reduction platforms and improved personal protective technologies. Finally, whenever clinically appropriate, non-ionizing imaging modalities should be considered as alternatives to conventional radiation-based techniques. The best way to protect your patients is to first protect yourself and your team. This proactive approach will ensure a longer, healthier personal and professional life while upholding the highest standard of patient care.
